                    ### Question
                    A 2-year-old girl presents to the emergency department with a 3-minute episode of a tonic-clonic seizure. The parents deny any previous history of seizure involving the patient or the family. Physical examination reveals an afebrile, well-groomed, and playful appearance, with normal vital signs. The patient carries a pink birthmark on the right side of her face extending from the forehead to the zygomatic arch. Which of the following findings is most likely on a head CT of this patient?

                    ### Options
                    opa. A non-enhancing hemispheric lesion
opb. Intraparenchymal hemorrhage
opc. Prominent intraparenchymal white matter calcification
opd. Subependymal giant cell astrocytoma
ope. Subependymal nodule

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The clinical presentation of a 2-year-old girl with a tonic-clonic seizure, no family history of seizures, and a pink birthmark on the face is suggestive of Sturge-Weber syndrome. This syndrome is characterized by a facial port-wine stain (nevus flammeus) and neurological abnormalities, including seizures. The most common finding on a head CT in patients with Sturge-Weber syndrome is prominent intraparenchymal white matter calcification, often described as 'tram-track' calcifications. The reasoning chains correctly identify the association between the facial birthmark and Sturge-Weber syndrome, leading to the expected CT finding of prominent intraparenchymal white matter calcification. Other options, such as subependymal nodules or giant cell astrocytomas, are more characteristic of tuberous sclerosis, which is not suggested by the clinical presentation. Therefore, the most likely finding on a head CT for this patient is prominent intraparenchymal white matter calcification.
